types.AbeStart: Where Abe materialises when a level opens fresh, rather than through a door, well or save. It is also what brings the pause menu into existence. Its stored fields are never read; the position is the rectangle itself, plus the twelve units the engine nudges him right.
types.Bat: A cave bat that hangs waiting, then flies along an invisible rail and dives at whatever it runs into: no line of sight, just touch. One brush is enough for the whole colony: the first Bat to find a target sets every Bat in the game on it at once. Each attacks once, flies up and is gone, and none survives a screen change.
types.BeeSwarmHole: A hole that pumps out a fresh bee swarm on a timer, forever, while you stand on its screen. Parking the rolling boulder over it plugs it: the game checks for a RollingBall covering the hole before every spawn. The game places exactly one, in the Paramonian Temple.
types.Bees: A wasps' nest, though the game's files call them wasps and players call them bees. A few drift around it harmlessly; trip its switch and it boils over into an angry swarm that hunts you until its chase timer runs out, stinging everything it envelops on the way. When the swarm dies the nest writes its own switch back off and re-arms.
types.BellHammer: The hammer-and-bell rig that calls Elum down from wherever he is. It watches its own switch id and clears it back to zero after every swing (a doorbell button, not a state), and finishing the swing spawns Elum if he isn't already in the world, dropped in just off-screen. An expensive object: it preloads all of Elum's animation banks just in case.
types.BellSongStone: The carved temple stone that sings a tune at Abe: hearing it is how he learns the song a chime lock wants. The tune is written as decimal digits across its two code fields (1 high whistle, 2 low, 3 fart), its type field decides whether the same digits play as whistles or chimes, and its switch id is the "Abe has heard this" flag a ChimeLock reads. Four stones set switch 0 or 1 (which sets nothing) and have no lock behind them: pure teaching stones.
types.BirdPortal: The ring of doves Abe chants open. A travel portal lifts him elsewhere on the map (the only kind that carries a destination), a worker portal opens the sky for Mudokons to escape into, and a Shrykull portal counts them: its number is a countdown, and at zero the doves pour back into Abe as lightning. It won't open with anyone standing too close; the doves scatter instead.
types.BirdPortalExit: The far end of a travel portal: the spot where Abe drops back out of the sky. The exit, not the entrance, decides the arrival (which way Abe faces and at what scale), and only the first exit in a camera is ever used. Both games place slightly fewer exits than travel portals.
types.BoomMachine: The grenade vending machine: a wall button with a nozzle that drops grenades while Abe's hands are empty. The button's light is exactly "is his throwable inventory empty", recomputed every frame, with no switch involved. Oddysee's machines dispense one to nine per press; every Exoddus machine gives exactly one.
types.BrewMachine: The SoulStorm Brew dispenser: a button with a two-digit counter, each serving one charge of the evil fart Abe can possess and detonate. The count survives leaving the screen (written into the marker itself), and two of the eleven machines ship empty from the start.
types.ChimeLock: The floating ball before three temple bells: possess it and ring them. Until Abe has heard the matching song stone the lock cannot be solved by hand (every manual note resets the progress), and once he has, it solves itself, playing its own code out one bell at a time. Five Scrabanian locks share one heard-the-song flag, so hearing any one stone unlocks all five.
types.ContinuePoint: The invisible checkpoint: walk through and the game quietly saves. In Oddysee it is zone-numbered (re-entering the same zone doesn't re-save) and stores the spot and facing you'll restart with; in Exoddus it is a one-shot quicksave trigger whose scale field is a filter that reads inverted, firing Half for a full-scale Abe and Full for a half-scale one, so one screen can checkpoint each plane separately.
types.ContinueZone: A large invisible region tagged with a checkpoint's zone number, and the engine never reads one. All 508 sit in the data as the designers' own map of which checkpoint governs where, the single largest population of inert objects in Oddysee. The respawn spot the game actually uses lives on the ContinuePoint.
types.CrawlingSlig: A Slig with no legs, dragging itself along the floor: no gun, no attack, just a desperate crawl toward a locker where it stands up armed. Every one the game fields starts asleep, and half wake straight into the scramble; their panic switch is the always-on id 1. Its crawl direction is decided once, when it spawns, and Random is a single coin flip rather than wandering.
types.CrawlingSligButton: A floor button only a player-driven Crawling Slig can press: Abe can't, and a crawling slig's own AI never looks for one. The game places exactly one, and pressing it always makes a noise Sligs and Slogs hear, whatever its switch does.
types.DeathClock: The countdown clock over the gas chamber, counting 02:00 down to zero. The 120 seconds are hardcoded, and so is its stop switch: id 70, a literal in the engine with no field behind it; the Board Room's lever on that id is what shuts it off. At zero the gas rises, visibly, and turns lethal three seconds later; all seven displays read one shared timer.
types.DeathDrop: The invisible "a fall from here is fatal" box under a bottomless drop: whatever touches it dies with the long scream-and-fall rather than a splat. Nearly every creature honours it (Abe's own fall broadcasts noise on the way down, so dying can give him away), and its stored words are dead data in both games, zero in every placement. In Exoddus the Mines' mine car crosses them safely.
types.Door: The doorway Abe steps through, one end of a pair: it names its partner's screen and door number, matched only inside the destination camera. That per-camera matching is why door numbers repeat freely across a level. The switch inverts the authored state rather than setting it (start open plus switch on means closed), and a gate door ANDs its eight hub ids into its own switch id; the first time all eight land plays the secret-music sting, in Oddysee on every gate door and in Exoddus only on the secret-music kind.
types.DoorBlocker: The lock hanging on a vault door, and it doesn't block: it explains. It has no collision and nothing consults it; the door beside it is what's shut. When its switch comes on it plays its unlocking animation once and is gone; 24 of the 25 watch the same switch as a tasks door on their path, popping the moment the tasks are done.
types.DoorFlame: A switch-controlled flame, and not a hazard: it does no damage and blocks nothing, and nothing in either engine can even find it by type. It is the tell that a switch state changed, dressed as fire. Strictly tribal, too: every placement in both games sits in a temple, a vault or Necrum, never an industrial level.
types.Dove: The white birds pecking about outdoors: noise scares them, and one bird's panic launches every dove on the screen, not just its own marker's. While any dove lives it holds the birdsong sequence open, so the ambience is literally the birds' presence. The same class circles bird portals, six at a time.
types.Drill: The industrial drill punching out of a wall or ceiling and back, Bonewerkz's and the Brewery's signature hazard. Its behavior field picks three machines: a free-running cycler, a switch-gated drill that can stop dead or merely slow to its off speed, and a one-stroke-per-use drill that resets its own switch. A speed of exactly 250 is special-cased to the slowest crawl in the game: the decompilation marks it a mystery, and fifteen drills rely on it.
types.Edge: The lip of a ledge Abe catches on the way down, not something you climb to but the edge you grab as you fall past. In both games a falling grab checks the Edge before the hoist (a no-grab Edge parked on a hoist blocks the falling catch) and a run-jump checks the hoist first. The direction is the way Abe must be facing to catch it.
types.ElectricWall: The crackling barrier across a doorway: touch it and you are electrocuted on the spot. Read start_state as the switch value at which the wall is not there (the common authored case is live until a switch kills it), and the buzz you hear near one is a real warning band, checked fifty units out on either side. Every wall in both games answers a real switch; none is hardwired.
types.ElumPathTrans: Permission for Elum to follow Abe off this screen. On a path change, Elum standing on one whose level and path match where you're going comes along; anywhere else he is left behind. He arrives a beat later, teleported in behind Abe at the screen's edge. All 28 sit in Paramonia and Scrabania, the only levels he travels.
types.ElumStart: The best misnomer in Oddysee's data: Elum does not start here; his own spawn is elsewhere. What this marks is the bell: Abe hopping into the wall where one sits gets a bell ring on top of the usual thud. Both placements share their screen with a BellHammer.
types.ElumWall: A resource hint wearing an object's clothes: it makes the game load Elum's crash animations for the screen, and nothing else. The wall itself would stop him regardless: he'd just have no artwork for the smack. All 23 sit in Paramonia, Scrabania and Monsaic Lines.
types.EnemyStopper: An invisible fence for creatures: Abe walks straight through, while patrols and chases stop, turn or give up at its line, each creature its own way. Its switch gate is inverted between the games: an Oddysee stopper blocks while its switch is off, an Exoddus one while it is on, so the permanent fence reads switch_id 0 in Oddysee and 1 in Exoddus.
types.ExplosionSet: The Mines bombardment. When the alarm meter runs out, the screen judders and a line of rocks marches across the area, one every third of a second, wrapping at the far edge; all fifteen placements are byte-identical, and none can start itself: each waits for the MinesAlarm the countdown meter creates. However many are placed, one object does the work: the rest re-tune it.
types.FallingItem: The thing that drops on your head (a boulder most places, a slab of meat in Rupture Farms, an exploding crate in Bonewerkz): the art is picked per level. It waits on its switch, falls, smashes and usually re-arms itself, setting its own switch back off on impact. In Rupture Farms one of them moonlights as the ambience: the level's meat-saw loop partly comes from its falling meat.
types.Fleech: A legless carnivore that sleeps until noise wakes it, then crawls after you faster than Abe can walk and drags its catch in with its tongue. Waking is an anger meter, not a trigger: walking feeds it, sneaking is genuinely silent. Only one Fleech in a level can eat at a time; the rest queue. It is one of the few things in either game that can eat a Mudokon.
types.FlintLockFire: The tribal fire-lighter: stone hammers and a gourd that strike a flame when their switch goes on. It is not a hazard, and nothing in it does damage. Lighting one plays the secret-area sting: a lit flintlock is the game telling you a secret paid off. Only three levels carry its artwork at all, and all fifteen placements sit exactly there.
types.FlyingSlig: A Slig in a hover rig, patrolling an invisible overhead rail and lobbing grenades (never bullets) at what it spots below. It hangs from a collision line rather than flying free, and only leaves the rail while possessed; hold the chant to let go and it blows itself up rather than hand the rig back. Unlike its walking cousin it ignores bound ids, leashing to whatever posts sit near its rail's ends.
types.FlyingSligSpawner: An invisible watcher that materialises one Flying Slig when its switch turns on, re-arming when that slig dies. Its fields are the stat sheet of the slig it will produce (the block is byte-identical to a placed Flying Slig's), and it writes its own switch back off on the slig's death, so anything else wired to the id sees the drop.
types.FootSwitch: The floor plate that fires once when something stands on it: stepping off pops the plate back up but leaves the switch where the press put it. Triggered-by Abe means Abe's own body: a possessed Slig can't press an Abe-only plate, but Abe's abandoned body standing on one does. Scales must match, so a background creature can't press a foreground plate. Oddysee's plates zero their switch every time the screen reloads; Exoddus' remember.
types.GasCountdown: Exoddus's escape clock: MM:SS on the wall, lethal gas at zero, the gas visible three seconds before it kills. Unlike Oddysee's hardcoded two minutes it reads its duration from a field, from four minutes in the Brewery Ender down to two seconds in FeeCo; its stop switch is wired to the never-on id 0 on every placement, so no shipped countdown can be stopped, only outrun.
types.GasEmitter: A gas nozzle that puffs coloured smoke and hisses: decoration for the gas sequences; the damage comes from the countdown, not the nozzle. Banks of them puff out of step by a random phase. Exoddus adds a colour field with five tints and ships every one of them yellow, plus a switch of its own, so a nozzle can be pure atmosphere with no clock anywhere.
types.Glukkon: In Exoddus, the industrialist boss class: he cannot hurt you at all. He screams, and his scream writes a switch that summons what can. Possess him and his voice commands Sligs; three placements are the named executives with their own movie deaths. Oddysee's six Glukkons are something else entirely: scenery behind the Board Room glass, jeering until the ending Shrykulls them.
types.GlukkonSwitch: The intercom only a Glukkon can talk to. It hails the character you're driving with a Glukkon "Hey"; answer "Do It" in a Glukkon's voice and it toggles its ok switch, and hailing it again toggles the switch back. Answering in the wrong voice would set the fail switch, but every shipped one leaves that id at zero, so being caught costs nothing but the sneer. Fumbling the Glukkon vocabulary is always free.
types.Greeter: A wheeled security machine sweeping a motion-detector beam ahead of itself. Cross the beam while moving and it charges and electrocutes; hold still and it rolls past. It carries its own detector rather than answering a placed one, and its start direction is wired backwards: Left starts it rolling right.
types.HandStone: The hand-print stone: press a palm to it and the camera flies off to show you somewhere else, up to three views. Oddysee's stones could name any screen in the game, each view a full level/path/camera triple, though every shipped one looks within its own path; Exoddus' name cameras within your path by construction. Ten Exoddus stones also write a switch when touched, so a look can open a door.
types.HintFly: The swarm of flies that spells a hint in mid-air, word by word, while Abe chants at it. Its message field indexes a 36-entry table the game carries (eleven messages are never placed, among them ABE WAS HERE and TEST THREE), and the swarm's size is allocated from the longest word it will ever need to spell.
types.Hoist: A ledge Abe grabs and pulls himself onto. The ones leading off the top of the screen trickle little rocks (that dust is the game saying there's a ledge up there) and grabbing one changes the camera. In Oddysee the marker's width is also its depth plane: wider than 18 units is foreground, 18 or less is background, because the field block has no scale of its own. In Exoddus, Fleeches climb them too.
types.HoneyDripTarget: A single aiming dot: the hanging honey sack in its camera drips its honey exactly here. Only one exists, under the Paramonia hive Elum can't leave alone. The game's other honey sack has no target anywhere in its level, so its drips land unseen at the path's corner.
types.IdSplitter: A wiring box with no presence in the world: one switch in, four out. Flipping the input toggles all four outputs after a delay; flipping it back toggles them again. It is the same machinery Exoddus ships as TimerTrigger, under Oddysee's own name for it; eleven of the twelve fan out instantly.
types.InvisibleSwitch: An unmarked trip zone: the game's tripwire. Walk the character you're driving into the box and, after its delay, a switch flips; some also sound the alarm that panics every Slig on the level. A pending delay survives a screen change, a door transition never trips it, and its scale field filters who can trip it rather than sizing anything.
types.InvisibleZone: A patch of shadow: with your whole body inside, enemies can't see you; a foot sticking out and you're visible, and chanting cancels the cover outright. Oddysee's Sligs are the only things that honour it; Exoddus adds Flying Sligs and Glukkons.
types.KillUnsavedMuds: The point of no return for Rupture Farms' Mudokons. Reaching its screen sets the killed count to 28 minus however many you saved (the 28 is hardcoded in the engine), and those totals pick your ending. Placed exactly once, in the Stock Yards, firing once and never again.
types.LaughingGas: A rectangle of drifting yellow haze, procedurally rendered: no sprite exists. Only Mudokons react, and only on the current screen: the haze turns them Wired, dropping whatever work they were doing. Its red, green and blue fields are dead (the constructor even copies blue into the green slot, a faithful original bug nothing can see), and the same object can be authored as harmless white mist, a branch no shipped placement uses.
types.LevelLoader: A scene-ender: when its switch comes on, the screen fades out and the game moves you where it names, movie and all; nobody has to touch anything. Exactly one exists, the Mines' six-wheel combination lock: its switch is written by the WheelSyncer whose six wheel inputs must all be on.
types.Lever: Exoddus's lever and the most-placed switch in either game. Same yank as Oddysee's, two upgrades and one stealth change: it can persist off-screen so a pull finishes while the camera moves, it snaps itself to the floor, and the noise enemies hear moved inside the sound cases; a lever with no sound wired (most of them) alerts nobody, where every Oddysee pull was heard.
types.LiftMover: The machinery that calls a lift with nobody aboard. Switch on and the lift it targets (paired by lift point id) travels the way the mover names, stopping at the first floor movers may use (a middle floor can opt out); switch off and it comes back. Invisible, and collision-free.
types.LiftMudokon: The one Mudokon in the game who walks in, works a lift for Abe, and walks away: a one-shot helper, not a resident. His lift id is a pairing number matching a LiftPoint, not a switch, and though he can be authored to teach a password, the single placed one never does.
types.LiftPoint: Both the lift platform and the floors it stops at. The marker flagged start point becomes the platform, the rest are stops (top, bottom or middle) whose type the platform adopts as it passes; the platform is real moving geometry, pinning everyone aboard to its line, even when its start point sits screens away up the shaft.
types.LocalWell: A hole that flings Abe across the screen, with two landing spots, one for each state of its switch. Exoddus wells compute a ballistic arc to the named landing point (Oddysee's threw raw velocities instead) and draw nothing themselves; the artwork is the level's. A local well can also be the arrival end of an express ride: its well number is what an express names.
types.MeatSaw: Rupture Farms' ceiling saw, dropping on its rig and rising again; it grinds anything it touches, except Meat itself. Its type field picks three machines: a free-running cycler, a two-tempo saw whose switch changes its speed rather than stopping it, and a one-stroke-per-trigger saw that writes its own switch back at each stroke's top. It survives a camera away, which is why you hear a saw before you see it.
types.Mine: The floor mine: a squat proximity bomb that ticks red and detonates on contact, the most common hazard in either game. It only answers its own plane: a background mine ignores a foreground Abe standing over it, and vice versa. A field of them ticks once, not fifty times (a single mine owns the ticking sound at any moment), and one that detonated never comes back, while one that merely despawned does.
types.MineCar: The rolling ore car Abe climbs into and becomes: he drives it along the rails and it flattens whatever it meets, taking no damage from anything. He can only climb out while it's parked facing up. The game fields three (two in the Mines, one in Bonewerkz) and its max_damage field is read by nothing.
types.MotionDetector: The red laser sweeping a corridor: move through it and the alarm sounds; hold perfectly still and it passes over you. The sizzle you hear as it crosses you is not the trip: motion is. The beam turns solid red the frame something is caught in it, and in Exoddus a detector with its flare hidden cannot trip at all, while Oddysee's two hidden ones are invisible and live.
types.MovieHandStone: A hand stone that plays a movie instead of showing a camera. It is resolved before HandStone when Abe touches a stone, its movie number indexes the current level's own film table (the same number means different films in different levels), and touching it writes its trigger switch like a HandStone's.
types.MovingBomb: A bomb that hums along its collision line like a travelling security orb, exploding on whatever it meets. Most start rolling the moment they spawn (wired to the always-on switch), and the hum drops to a whisper when you are far away. Its max_rise field is dead data in both games, plausible-looking values and all.
types.MovingBombStopper: A pause zone painted on a moving bomb's route: the bomb slows into it, waits a random beat between the stopper's min and max, and rolls on. No switch, no id: it works purely by the bomb standing in it. Exoddus ships the type and reads it faithfully, but places none: every Exoddus bomb runs nonstop.
types.Mudokon: A worker: the ones you are here to rescue. Greet one and it follows until you point it at a bird portal; the rescue itself flips its rescue switch on, which is how a level can react to that particular worker getting out. Oddysee's carry a job and can be deaf; Exoddus' are a bigger machine (moods that reshape every response, blindness, depression, laughing gas that turns them Wired, sick ones cured by a healing ring), and only one Mudokon answers a shout at a time: the nearest.
types.MudokonPathTrans: A patch of floor where a Mudokon you're leading may cross a path boundary with you; anywhere else, changing path leaves it behind. Its three destination fields are never read; the marker's presence is the entire signal. Placed exactly once, in Rupture Farms.
types.MultiSwitchController: The timed AND gate behind Exoddus's hit-them-all rooms. Six input switches must all come on within its window of the first: miss it and every input is wiped to zero to start you over; land it and the action fires at the output id. Unused inputs are wired to the always-on id 1, which excludes them from both the timing and the punishment.
types.Paramite: A spider-crab that hisses a warning before it charges, and drops in on a silk thread from off-screen. Thrown meat distracts an idle one but never one already chasing; alone it hesitates, with another Paramite on the screen it commits. In Exoddus it can be possessed and climbs the web lines, and it obeys a possessed Paramite's calls: Paramites listen to Paramites, never to Abe.
types.ParamiteWebLine: The hanging web strand a Paramite climbs, but only its artwork. The climbable part is a track line the level already carries; the strand finds that line, drapes itself along it, and wobbles when a Paramite grabs on. Abe can't touch it: riding one means possessing a Paramite. All 25 hang in Mudomo Vault.
types.PathTransition: An invisible patch at a screen's edge that redirects the walk-off: instead of scrolling to the neighbour, you are sent to the level, path and camera it names. Oddysee leans on these for its outdoor walk-offs (56 against Exoddus' 9) and in Oddysee the crossing rescales anything that walks over it, not just Abe.
types.PullRingRope: The ring on a rope: grab it, drop with your weight, and the switch flips. Oddysee applies the flip the instant you grab, and its on/off sound fields can never play: an original bug left their trigger comparing against an operation that never happens; Exoddus flips at the end of the pull instead, so dying mid-pull leaves the switch untouched, and there a Paramite can pull one too.
types.Pulley: The wheel at the top of a lift shaft, sometimes screens above the lift, which is normal rather than a mistake: the platform goes looking for it. The Exoddus platform climbs camera rows; the Oddysee one checks its own camera and the one above. Only its position is read; wheel and ropes anchor there, and a lift with no pulley runs its ropes to the top of the screen.
types.ResetSwitchRange: An invisible line that wipes a whole block of switch ids back to zero when Abe crosses it, only Abe: a possessed body walking over it does nothing. All twelve fire once (the misnamed enabled field means repeatable, and none enables it), and six also have the wipe itself switched off, so crossing those six does nothing measurable at all.
types.RingCancel: An invisible box that takes Abe's spirit ring away, so a ring earned in one place can't be carried into the next. Two of the ten placed strip Shrykull instead, because the original engine read two bytes past the record's end and found garbage that happened to be non-zero; the decompilation reproduces both by address.
types.RingMudokon: A temple Mudokon who chants a spirit ring into Abe (or pulls a lever for him) once he's said Hello back, teaching the password first if asked. Eight of the eleven give rings and three pull levers, and only one ring in the game is on a timer, a Scrabania mud's at 800 frames; every other ring lasts until spent or revoked.
types.RollingBall: The temple boulder, waiting for its release switch. Rolling, it crushes without any filter (no scale check, no type check, everything in the way) and the engine special-cases its famous ending: in the Paramonian Temple the long fall parks it exactly on the bee hole, plugging the swarm for good. Two exist, both in that temple.
types.RollingBallStopper: The wedge holding the boulder back, a real wall of dynamic collision, one-sided: it only holds a ball rolling one way. Its switch goes on, the wedge tumbles away, and once it has fallen far enough it writes the ball's release switch itself: a genuine producer, stopper switch in, ball switch out. The game places exactly one.
types.Scrab: A two-legged carnivore that paces between its bound posts and kills what it reaches in one hit. Two Scrabs that see each other fight, and the duel is decided by which one's turn comes first in the engine's update order, not by strength. In Exoddus Abe can possess one; finishing a howl charges the spin attack, and spending it costs the charge.
types.ScrabLeftBound: The left end of a ground creature's beat: pace into it and turn back. Unlike a Slig's posts these carry no id (a creature takes whichever bound it walks into), and only the patrol honours them; a chasing Scrab crosses its own leash freely. In Exoddus they pen more than Scrabs: Glukkons, Greeters and Slurgs all turn at them, and 23 of the 56 pairs sit in levels with no Scrab at all.
types.ScrabNoFall: Despite the name it doesn't forbid falling: it authorises jumping. A chasing Scrab takes a running leap at the end of its ground when its prey is level with it, or when one of these markers sits ahead saying jump anyway; with neither, it runs off the edge and falls. Only the chase reads it.
types.ScrabRightBound: The right end of a ground creature's beat: pace into it and turn back. It carries no id and pairs with no particular creature, so the patrolling Scrab (or, in Exoddus, Glukkon, Greeter or Slurg) simply turns at whichever post it meets, and a chase crosses it freely.
types.ScrabSpawner: A switch-triggered Scrab factory carrying a full Scrab stat sheet of its own. It keeps exactly one Scrab in flight at a time: the next spawns only when the last is gone, the spawner writing its own switch back off in between. The game fields exactly one, in Mudanchee Vault.
types.SecurityClaw: Rupture Farms' hanging claw: it slides along its rail (the marker's rect) to stay above Abe, delivering the chanting zap with jaws around it. Its second job is the alarm: gunfire or an explosion in its screen makes it raise one, setting its alarm switch. It even adopts every motion detector on its screen and carries them as it moves. Exoddus's two reuse the id for an armed chant suppressor the decompilation leaves unimplemented.
types.SecurityDoor: The Slig-voice password panel: it hails you, recites a passphrase in Slig grunts, and opens (setting its switch) only for a correct repeat, in Slig. A solved panel stays solved; a half-finished conversation resets. Oddysee's panels speak four Slig words to Exoddus's three.
types.SecurityOrb: The humming eye that punishes chanting. It listens for the chant itself (not motion, not sight) and a beat later zaps Abe's own body, wherever the possessed one stands; the hum is the whole warning system. Destructible, and destroyed for good. In Exoddus a Shrykull-charged Abe chants past one untouched; Oddysee's make no exception.
types.SlamDoor: The heavy slab that seals a corridor: real geometry while shut (it owns two collision walls) and nothing at all while open. Closing on someone shoves them clear, and hurts Abe and Mudokons; a slam door with its delete flag set opens once and never comes back. Crawling Sligs, Scrabs, Fleeches and Glukkons read its marker rather than the object, so a shut one turns them around; a walking Slig is stopped by the door's own walls instead.
types.SlapLock: A shuddering spirit lock that only Abe's slap can break. Ghost-guarded ones free a spirit that flies to the tomb door named by one target field and sets the switch named by the other on arrival; a broken lock holding the invisibility power-up respawns as a permanent dispenser of it.
types.Slig: The gun-toting guard on stilts, the games' signature enemy: it patrols between its bound posts and shoots what it sees on its own plane of the world. Its start_state is the field to read, and the value labelled listening is really a stationary sentry: it holds its post and fires the moment you step in front of it. A sleeping one snores audibly from the neighbouring screen (the ambience is read straight off this marker before any Slig exists), and a blast reaching the marker kills it sight unseen, the gibs flying in from off-screen.
types.SligBoundLeft: The left post of a Slig's patrol pen: a Slig carrying the matching id turns short of this post's line and never walks past it. The post does two quieter jobs too: it loads the Slig animation sets for its camera, and it can conjure its matching Slig onto your screen from a camera away, which is how one walks in from off-screen.
types.SligBoundRight: The right post of a Slig's patrol pen: a Slig carrying the matching id turns short of this post's line and never walks past it. Both games place slightly fewer right posts than left, so some Sligs are fenced on one side only.
types.SligGetPants: A locker of Slig trousers: a Crawling Slig that reaches it climbs in and walks out a full armed Slig. The locker's own fields are the stat sheet of the Slig it produces (the transformation reads them, not the crawler's), and if the crawler was possessed, you carry over into the new body.
types.SligGetWings: A locker stocked with a hover rig instead of trousers. The Crawling Slig that reaches it flies out as a Flying Slig, drifting upward until it catches a rail to latch onto; its fields are that slig's stat sheet, and the game fields exactly one.
types.SligPersist: A leash pin that keeps a Slig alive off-camera. A Slig sharing its id survives while any of its pins is on the current screen, instead of despawning when it walks out of view; Exoddus leans on these harder than Oddysee, placing more pins than it places Sligs.
types.SligSpawner: A marked spot that materialises a Slig when its switch turns on, and since its field block is a Slig's, a spawner tells you exactly what is coming. In Oddysee every spawner is single-shot; in Exoddus 30 of the 32 re-arm each time their slig dies, writing the switch back off as they do. Spawner Sligs skew hard toward Chase, a start state placed Sligs barely use: spawners are how the games deliver Sligs that arrive already hunting.
types.SlingMudokon: The Monsaic guardian who fades in from nothing, whistles a password, and waits for Abe to repeat it; approach instead of answering and the sling comes out. On a correct answer he leaves as eight doves. All four placements teach their code; the ask-me-first variant the fields allow never ships.
types.Slog: The slavering guard dog with a fatal bite. Its three anger fields stack as increments (wake at wake_up_anger, bark that much plus bark_anger, charge past the sum of all three) fed by noise, speech and Abe standing close; one thrown-object hit adds the whole charge threshold at once. A Slig (which is to say, you possessing one) can whistle it to heel or set it on someone with "get 'em", the only way its own search ever picks out a Slig; a spawner-born Slog simply hunts whatever you are possessing.
types.SlogHut: Not a hut and not a Slog: a particle emitter puffing sleep-Zs while its switch is off. Every one in the game shares its switch with a SlogSpawner: the Zs mark the kennel while the switch is off, and the moment it flips the Zs stop and the paired spawner starts pouring out Slogs.
types.SlogSpawner: A Slog fountain: while its switch is on it releases Slogs on a timer, up to a lifetime quota that survives leaving the screen. Its at-a-time cap counts every live Slog, not just its own (neighbouring spawners share one ceiling), and each Slog it births arrives already hunting, on fixed anger numbers rather than a placed Slog's.
types.Slurg: A fat slug that inches along the floor and bursts with a wet pop under anyone's step: Abe's, a Mudokon's, a Slig's, a Scrab's. It can't hurt anything; the danger is the pop itself, a loud noise, and loud noises are what wake Fleeches. Its switch field is a kill counter (each burst adds one), and eleven Slurgs ship wired to one.
types.SlurgSpawner: A crack that dribbles out Slurgs on a timer, up to a lifetime quota that survives leaving the screen: a spawner that has met its five stays spent. The game places exactly one, in Mudanchee Vault, wired to the always-on switch: it never stops until the quota is met.
types.SoftLanding: A patch of ground safe to hit from any height: land inside it and the fall that would kill just stings. Exoddus gates it on a switch for Abe (one shipped zone is wired permanently off) while its Sligs and Mudokons are spared unconditionally, so a zone can be off for Abe and on for everyone else.
types.Switch: The wall lever Abe grabs and yanks, flipping the switch id it is wired to. The flip lands on the pull animation's last frame, every pull makes a noise Sligs can investigate, and the on/off sounds are the machinery being operated, played only when the value actually changed, so a lever can sound like a door once and never again. Commanded Mudokons and possessed Sligs pull them too.
types.Teleporter: A ring of electricity: any change to its switch, on or off, zaps whoever stands in it to the partner ring, resizing them to the destination's scale. It moves the controlled character, so a possessed body rides it too. Its tp numbers are pair ids matched inside the destination camera, not switch states, despite the field names.
types.TimedMine: A bomb that does nothing until Abe slaps it, then counts down and explodes, the tick accelerating as the fuse runs out. Once armed it survives leaving the screen, so you can slap it and walk away. Oddysee places ten; Exoddus ships the whole working machine and places none.
types.TimerTrigger: The fan-out box: one input switch drives four outputs after a delay, on both edges. The input changing toggles all four; the input coming back toggles them back. The outputs are always toggled, never set, and a countdown in flight survives the screen changing. Half the placements use delay zero: a plain one-to-four splitter.
types.TorturedMudokon: A Mudokon strung up in a tear extractor, writhing out of sync with its neighbours: each starts on a random animation frame. It can't be led, only freed: its release switch stops the current for good, in groups that share one switch. A kill switch exists in the fields, wired to the never-on id 0 on every one, so no tortured Mudokon in the game can die by switch.
types.TrainDoor: The sliding door on the FeeCo train carriage: the graphic, not the ride. It names no destination and reads no switch; the ordinary Door beside it carries the travel. It waits for Abe to step out, then slides shut behind him for good.
types.TrapDoor: A hinged floor panel: solid ground while closed (a real platform with its own collision line) and a hole the moment its switch matches. A self-closing one writes its own switch back as it shuts, re-arming its trigger, and its dest_level field is dead data: every Exoddus door says Necrum Mines and not one means it.
types.UXB: The blinking bomb you disarm by timing a slap: green is safe, red is not. Its pattern field is decimal digits (each digit how many red blinks before the next green) though most Exoddus UXBs truncate theirs to a single digit through a mismatched pattern length. A disarmed one can be slapped again to re-arm it, and it remembers its state when you leave the screen.
types.Water: A curtain of falling water, purely cosmetic: it damages nothing. Its drops are a hand-managed particle pool capped at 128, and both placements ask for 300, so each is silently clipped. One leaks in the Mines and one in the Brewery, each on a real switch with a self-stop timer.
types.WellExpress: A well that ships you to another screen, often another level, with a destination for each state of its switch. Arrival is by well number, scanned inside the destination camera only (never by position), and a state can be a dead end, written either as the well naming its own id or as an address never filled in. In Monsaic Lines the temple rides are one-way: the engine remembers you rode one and bounces you back out ever after.
types.WellLocal: A hole that flings Abe across the screen, with two shots, one for each state of its switch. Oddysee's wells read the pair as a raw velocity, in hundredths per frame, and draw their own well artwork; the drifting leaves gate on the same switch. A local well can also be the arrival end of an express ride: its well number is what an express names.
types.WheelSyncer: A logic gate with no memory. Every frame it reads up to six inputs, applies its rule (all-on for 15 of the 18) and writes the answer straight into its output switch; nothing else can hold that output, whatever writes it is overwritten next frame. Unused inputs must be wired to the always-on id 1, or an all-on gate can never fire.
types.WorkWheel: The crank wheel: turn it long enough and the switch it drives comes on, and on two of the 100, keep cranking past their off time and you undo yourself. Most latch on; seventeen let go when you do. One wheel ends the game: the engine hardcodes that a Brewery Ender wheel on switch 100 starts the ending sequence, and exactly one such wheel exists.
types.ZBall: A pendulum swinging toward and away from the camera, in front of Abe and then behind him. Its damage rides the animation itself: only frames the artists marked can hit. Its start position (centre, out, in) staggers a row of balls out of phase. All six in the game hang in the Paramonian Temple.
types.ZSligCover: A no-fire zone for depth shooting: inside this rectangle a background Slig cannot snipe across the depth axis, and a Z-bullet that lands there is absorbed. It protects both ways (a Slig standing in cover won't fire out of it) but only whole-body: a box that half-covers you protects you not at all.
types.ZzzSpawner: A floating snore: it puffs a sleep-Z on a timer, knowing nothing about who sleeps below, so the author parks it over the sleeper. Its switch gate is inverted: Zs flow while the switch is off and stop when it turns on, which is why the sleeper's wake switch and the spawner's can be one number.
